thread.title: Apple WWDC: What It Means for Apple’s Stock

author: Jon Swartz
title: Apple WWDC: What It Means for Apple’s Stock
text:
Illustration: Ori Toor By Jon Swartz June 1, 2018 2:51 p.m. ET Few things ignite the passions of Apple investors more than the run-up to a new hardware announcement. It happens like clockwork: Shares rise in the months leading to the latest-and-greatest iPhone or iPad, usually in early September, before the inevitable selloff on the news.
The same holds true, to a lesser extent, for the annual Apple Worldwide Developers Conference, or WWDC, which begins this year on June 4 in San Jose, Calif. The conference is focused on software, but the broader mission is to sell Apple’s ecosystem to software developers, while providing a road map for what consumers and businesses can expect in terms of hardware over the coming year.
Apple (ticker: AAPL) enters the five-day conference with investor faith restored and the stock near an all-time high. Investors have put aside concerns about iPhone sales to focus on Apple’s capital-return program. Last month, Apple boosted its buyback program, authorizing another $100 billion for share repurchases, and raised its dividend by 16%.
Apple’s Appeal? It’s Sexual The gadget maker's popularity is based firmly in reproductive instincts, argues NYU professor Scott Galloway. After several years in which the stock looked historically cheap, Apple trades at 14.8 times consensus earnings estimates for the next 12 months. That’s just above the stock’s 10-year average of 14.4. But for all of the excitement about buybacks, Apple still trades at a discount to the broad market; the S&P 500 fetches a forward multiple of 16.3.
Barron’s has been bullish on Apple stock , mainly because investors could keep pushing Apple’s valuation higher, particularly as the company taps into its powerful ecosystem, generating a stream of recurring services revenue.
But this year’s WWDC could also serve to remind investors that Apple remains a leader in innovation, even as the iPhone—which accounts for about 60% of annual revenue—remains a nagging issue. Sales have been good, but not spectacular. Apple’s 14.1% first-quarter share of the global smartphone market (54.1 million units sold) is second to Samsung Electronics , but only marginally better than the year-ago quarter, according to market researcher Gartner. In her annual report on internet trends this week, Mary Meeker, a partner at venture-capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, said 2017 was the first year that smartphone unit shipments didn’t grow.
Apple could assuage concerns next week with new features in augmented reality, artificial intelligence, and cross-platform app development for the iPhone and its Mac computer line. Daniel Ives, head of technology research at GBH Insights, believes those features, combined with new iPhones expected in September, will rejuvenate iPhone sales and excite Wall Street. He anticipates a “massive” upgrade cycle from a pool of roughly 350 million iPhones over the next 12 to 18 months. Any positive iPhone news would solidify Apple’s path to a $1 trillion market value, which requires a share price of $197, 5% above a recent close of $187.
Apple didn’t respond to messages seeking comment about its WWDC plans, but developers, industry experts, and tech analysts offered Barron’s a look at what to expect. The most promising development is Apple’s embrace of “cross-platform functionality,” which would let developers create apps that work on both iPhones and Macs.
“For developers, this leads to a lot for bang for the buck,” says Nate Frechette, co-founder and chief technology officer at mobile app platform Dropsource, an Apple developer. “It has been a pain to develop for different platforms.” Aside from saving developers time and money, cross-platform functionality frees them to create universal apps in emerging fields such as AR and AI.
Last year, Apple unveiled ARKit, a new technology that lets its army of developers create AR apps for hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Apple CEO Tim Cook, generally a laid-back executive, gets unusually excited when talking about AR .
“AR has the ability to amplify human performance instead of isolating humans,” Cook said during Apple’s first-quarter earnings call in February. “So I am a huge, huge believer in AR. We put a lot of energy on AR. We’re moving very fast.”
And, yet, thus far the AR talk—also a major topic at last year’s WWDC—hasn’t amounted to much. Apple “raised the hype” on AR and “needs to take it to the next level,” says Tuong Nguyen, principal research analyst at Gartner. “They need to show a real-world application that resonates more broadly, a step beyond what we saw last year.”
Newsletter Sign-up The long-term path for AR development could be augmented-reality glasses, though that’s still a few years away, says Tim Bajarin, president at market researcher Creative Strategies. “AR, like Siri, requires new advancements as it integrates into the Apple ecosystem,” he says.
This year’s WWDC could also offer hope for Siri, which needs a kick-start to catch up with rival voice assistants from Amazon.com (AMZN) and Alphabet ’s (GOOGL) Google. Jonathan Matus, who worked on speech recognition at Google, expects Apple to expand machine-learning intelligence across Siri, while using new data sets to deliver more-refined search results. “Apple will make Siri more conversational with it integrated into powerful apps,” says Matus, the co-founder and CEO of mobile driving-analytics company Zendrive.
An improved Siri could drive the next leg of growth for platforms like iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Music, AppleCare, and iTunes. Apple’s services unit pulled in $33.4 billion in revenue over the past 12 months. That’s roughly in line with what Nike and Coca-Cola made, in total, last year. GBH’s Ives estimates Apple’s services revenue could reach $50 billion annually by 2020.
That growth could come down to what’s announced at next week’s WWDC, which “lays the groundwork and sets the tone for developers,” says Phil Libin, a co-founder of Evernote and the current CEO of AI start-up studio All Turtles.
Sure enough, previous WWDC announcements include the overhauled Mac operating system (1998), the original iPhone OS (2007), and the iPhone App Store (2008). Those could be the three most important pieces of software launched in the past 20 years.
